newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Britain, Ireland stick to N.Ireland timetable.
newsitem.headline: Britain, Ireland stick to N.Ireland timetable.

text.p: Britain and Ireland vowed on Tuesday to press ahead with substantive Northern Ireland peace talks in September despite deep reservations in the province's key Protestant unionist party.

Irish Foreign Minister Ray Burke and Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam said the two governments were determined to stick to the September timetable and hoped that unionists, who want to stay part of Britain, would join the negotiations.
"There is no Plan B. There is a Plan A," Burke told a news conference at the end of the morning talks. "What we want now is goodwill on all sides," he said.

He was responding to speculation that the two governments were drafting alternative plans for the year-long peace talks should they break down because of an unresolved dispute over the "decommissioning" or surrender of guerrilla arms.

Two unionist parties walked out of the talks altogether last week and the province's key pro-British group, David Trimble's Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), is staunchly against the current decommissioning plans.

Trimble said he would stay in the talks but is bitterly opposed to the Anglo-Irish plan to allow the IRA and its loyalist foes to disarm as the talks progress rather than at the start or end of the negotiations.
Burke and Mowlam said they would be holding talks with all parties, including the UUP, to ensure that negotiations began on September 9 with the first plenary session on September 15.
"I am an optimist. I believe in looking at the positive side rather than the negative. I have confidence people want them (all sides) to talk," Burke said.

Political sources said they doubted whether the UUP would sit at the same negotiating table as Sinn Fein, the political wing of the Irish Republican Army which has fought a 28-year war against British rule of Northern Ireland.
The UUP says the IRA called a ceasefire 10 days ago in a ruse to get Sinn Fein admitted to the negotiations when they resume. It sees the British stance on disarming the IRA as weak.
Irish and British officials said they had not ruled out starting the negotiations as "proximity talks", with the UUP and Sinn Fein negotiating under the same roof but not at the same table.
"We just want them there on the day to get this thing started," one Irish official said.
The two governments welcomed the IRA ceasefire and said it would be enough to admit Sinn Fein to the negotiations if Britain deems it genuine "in word and deed".
There have been no IRA attacks since the July 20 IRA ceasefire, which restored a truce the guerrillas broke in February 1996.
The two governments said they were pressing ahead with plans to set up a "decommissioning committee" to tackle the single biggest issue on the talks agenda.
They want all sides to agree that the IRA and pro-British loyalists, who called their own ceasefire in October 1994, should start surrendering weapons as talks proceed.
Some 3,200 people have been killed in the past three decades of conflict between Protestants and Roman Catholics in Northern Ireland.
